School counsellor's note, Tuesday

Today I met Vinita and her daughter Madhuri, after Madhuri lied about a weekend trip.
Vinita started by saying, "I'm hurt by the lie. And I also want to understand why you felt you couldn't ask me."
Madhuri was silent for a long time. Then she said, "Because I thought you'd say no, and then be angry for days."
Vinita looked shocked. "I didn't know you were afraid of me."
"Not afraid. Just… scared of the no."
They both went quiet. I asked each of them to say one thing they had just learned. Vinita said, "That my no's feel so final." Madhuri said, "That Mummy was hurt, not just angry."
We'll meet again next week.

qa.a: A weekend trip.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she explained why she lied?
qa.a: She was scared of her mother's no and of the anger that followed.

qa.q: What made this conversation work?
qa.a: Vinita named her hurt but also asked why Madhuri couldn't ask, which let Madhuri admit her fear, and the counsellor helped both say what they had learned.

qa.q: What was Vinita experiencing when she heard Madhuri's reason?
qa.a: She was shocked, realising that her no's felt so final to her daughter.

grounding: A counsellor records a mother naming her hurt and asking why her daughter couldn't ask, and both learn something unexpected.

Mumma found out about me and Siddharth going to the movie on Friday, when I'd said I was at Priyanka's.
I waited all day for the explosion. It didn't come.

Mumma put down her spoon. "I didn't know that. I thought you just didn't want to tell me things."

I didn't expect any of that. — Ankita

passage:
I'm Jagdish, Pema's uncle. I stay with them on weekends when I come down from Gangtok.
For six weeks now, I've watched Pema do small things. Every Saturday she tells her mother where she's going before she leaves. She's home when she says she will be. Last Sunday she even texted from the bus, "Running ten minutes late."
My sister hasn't noticed. She's still waiting for the next lie.
So last night I said to her, over dinner, "Pema has kept every promise for six weeks. I've been counting."
Pema looked up from her plate, surprised. My sister looked at her for a long moment. Then she said, "You're right. Thank you, Pema."
Pema smiled all through the dishes.

qa.q: How many weeks had Pema kept her promises?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he watched Pema's small actions?
qa.a: Jagdish felt proud and encouraged by Pema's reliability, and eager for her mother to see it.

qa.q: What difference did Jagdish's words make?
qa.a: By noting Pema's track record aloud, Jagdish helped her mother notice the pattern of honesty, which makes more honesty likely.

qa.q: What was Pema experiencing when her mother thanked her?
qa.a: She felt surprised and happy, smiling all through the dishes because her honesty had been noticed.

grounding: An uncle observes his niece keep small promises for weeks and says so aloud to her mother, helping honesty be noticed.

Suraj, you want to know how your Papa and your Dadi became close again when he was your age? I'll tell you. I'm Anand, his mama, and I saw it.
Your Papa, at fifteen, had lied about a cricket match in another town. Your Dadi stopped believing anything he said.
That summer I stayed with them. And I watched. Every day he said where he was going. Every evening he was home on time. He even told her when he broke a glass.
After a month, I said to your Dadi, "He's kept every word for four weeks. Have you noticed?" She hadn't. She looked at him, surprised.
He stood up straighter after that. He kept being honest, because now someone was noticing.
